lesson.lead: SVM uses three ideas from earlier topics. Each has its own part next (P1–P3) with the slides to read and YouTube videos to watch. If you can already do the quick check at the bottom, skip them.

items: **P1 · Vectors:** dot product wᵀx, length ‖w‖, orthogonality, distance from a point to a line. Slides: MFML `Lecture_3.pdf` (Prof. Saurabh → Lecture_Slides). Used in every SVM numerical.

lesson.title: P1 · Vectors: dot product, norm, distance
lesson.lead: Source: MFML `Lecture_3.pdf` (Prof. Saurabh → Lecture_Slides). Four facts, each with the slide that prints it.

blocks.text: 1. Dot product
xᵀy = x₁y₁ + x₂y₂ + … + xₙyₙ
blocks.caption: Slide: *Inner Products* (p. 5)

blocks.text: Example: (3, 4)ᵀ(4, 2) = 12 + 8 = **20**. In SVM, wᵀx + b is this dot product plus a number.
2. Length (norm)
‖x‖ = {{sqrt: x₁² + x₂² + … + xₙ²}} = {{sqrt: xᵀx}}
blocks.caption: Slides: *Norms* (p. 4, Euclidean norm) and *Lengths and Distances* (p. 9)

blocks.text: Example: ‖(3, 4)‖ = {{sqrt: 9 + 16}} = **5**. In SVM the margin is 2/‖w‖, so ‖w‖ = 5 gives margin 0.4.
3. Orthogonal means dot product 0
x ⊥ y  ⇔  xᵀy = 0
blocks.caption: Slide: *Angles and Orthogonality* (p. 16)

blocks.text: Why SVM needs it: w is perpendicular to the line wᵀx + b = 0. Take two points xₐ, x_{b} on the line; subtracting gives wᵀ(xₐ − x_{b}) = 0. Slide: MFML `Lecture_14.pdf` (Prof. Saurabh → Lecture_Slides), *Hyperplane* (p. 13).
4. Distance from a point to a line
distance of x₀ from wᵀx + b = 0  =  |wᵀx₀ + b| / ‖w‖
blocks.caption: Not printed on L3. One-line derivation below.

items: Walk from x₀ towards the line along the unit normal w/‖w‖ (fact 3) for a distance t: the foot is x₀ − t·w/‖w‖.
The foot is on the line: wᵀ(x₀ − t·w/‖w‖) + b = 0 ⇒ wᵀx₀ + b − t·‖w‖ = 0 (since wᵀw = ‖w‖², fact 2).
So t = (wᵀx₀ + b)/‖w‖; distance = its absolute value.

blocks.label: Link to SVM
blocks.text: A point on the margin line wᵀx + b = +1 is |1|/‖w‖ from the boundary; one on −1 is also 1/‖w‖ away. Total gap = **2/‖w‖**, the margin (SVM slide *Linear SVM Mathematically*, p. 16).

lesson.title: P2 · Linear classifier: a line and a sign
lesson.lead: Sources: ML `ML_CS 5 6.pdf` (Session PPTs) and MFML `Lecture_14.pdf` (Prof. Saurabh → Lecture_Slides).

blocks.text: f(x, w) = w₀ + wᵀx,   y = sign(w₀ + wᵀx),   boundary: w₀ + wᵀx = 0
blocks.caption: Slide: *Decision Rules* (ML CS 5–6, p. 9). The SVM slides write b instead of w₀: same thing.

items: **The boundary** is a line in 2-D (a plane in 3-D, a hyperplane in general).
**The sign** decides the class: f > 0 ⇒ +1, f < 0 ⇒ −1.
**w** points towards the + side (it is perpendicular to the line, P1 fact 3). **b** shifts the line without turning it.

blocks.text: Logistic regression uses the same line: on the boundary its output is 0.5 (slide *Logistic Regression – Sample Linear Boundary*, p. 14).

blocks.label: Link to SVM
blocks.text: Many lines separate the same data. The slides *Linear Classifier for Binary Classification* and *Linear Classifier* (MFML L14, p. 20–24) draw several. SVM chooses the one with the **widest gap** to the nearest points. That choice is the whole chapter.

lesson.title: P3 · Lagrange multipliers, dual and KKT
lesson.lead: Source: MFML `Lecture_14.pdf` (Prof. Saurabh → Lecture_Slides). Its agenda (p. 2) says it is the *Mathematical preliminaries for Support Vector Machines*. Practice: `Lagrange-KKT-Duality-Practice-Set.pdf` (Prof. Saurabh → practice_problems).

blocks.text: 1. The problem and its Lagrangian
minimise f(x)  subject to  gᵢ(x) ≤ 0,  hⱼ(x) = 0
blocks.caption: Slide: *Optimization problem* (p. 3)

blocks.text: L = f(x) + Σ λᵢ gᵢ(x) + Σ νⱼ hⱼ(x)
blocks.caption: Slide: *Optimization problem : Lagrangian* (p. 4). One multiplier per constraint.

blocks.text: 2. Recipe: set the derivative to 0, then use the constraint
Example (equality): minimise x² + y² subject to x + y = 2. Write h = x + y − 2.

items: L = x² + y² + ν(x + y − 2).
Constraint: x + y = 2 ⇒ −ν = 2 ⇒ ν = −2, so **x = y = 1**, minimum value 2.

blocks.text: The practice set writes this as ∇f = λ∇h, which gives λ = +2. That's the same answer with the opposite sign convention.
3. Inequality constraints: KKT
1. gᵢ(x*) ≤ 0, hⱼ(x*) = 0   2. λᵢ ≥ 0   3. λᵢ gᵢ(x*) = 0   4. ∇f + Σλᵢ∇gᵢ + Σνⱼ∇hⱼ = 0
blocks.caption: Slide: *KKT conditions* (p. 11). Condition 3 is complementary slackness.

blocks.text: Example: minimise x² subject to x ≥ 1, i.e. g = 1 − x ≤ 0. L = x² + λ(1 − x), so 2x − λ = 0.

blocks.label: Link to SVM
blocks.text: In SVM each training point gives one constraint yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 with multiplier αᵢ. Complementary slackness says **αᵢ > 0 only if the point sits exactly on the margin**. Those points are the support vectors. Every other point has αᵢ = 0.
4. Primal → dual, and when they agree

items: *Recall : Quadratic programming* (p. 5–7): for ½xᵀQx + cᵀx with Ax ≤ b, set ∂L/∂x = 0, substitute x back, and maximise the result D(λ) over λ ≥ 0. **The SVM primal (min ½‖w‖² with linear constraints) is exactly such a QP**, and this is how the SVM dual is built.
*Weak duality* (p. 8): dual optimum ≤ primal optimum.

*Strong duality* (p. 9) and *Slater's condition* (p. 10): convex objective, linear constraints, and a strictly feasible point ⇒ the two are equal. SVM satisfies this, so solving the dual gives the same w and b.

lesson.title: What SVM is, in simple terms
lesson.lead: A classifier that separates two groups with the widest possible empty road between them.

blocks.text: Watch first: SVM on YouTube

items: [▶ StatQuest · Support Vector Machines Part 1 (of 3): Main Ideas!](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=statquest+support+vector+machines+part+1+main+ideas): margin, support vectors, soft margin, all with pictures. Start here.

[▶ Visually Explained · Support Vector Machines: All you need to know!](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=visually+explained+support+vector+machines+all+you+need+to+know): the whole chapter in one sitting: margin, primal, dual, kernels.

[▶ MIT OCW 6.034 · 16. Learning: Support Vector Machines (Patrick Winston)](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=mit+6.034+16+learning+support+vector+machines+winston): derives 2/‖w‖, the Lagrangian and w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ on the board. The closest to the exam.

[▶ StatQuest · Support Vector Machines Part 2: The Polynomial Kernel](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=statquest+support+vector+machines+part+2+polynomial+kernel): (a·b + r)ᵈ and why it is a dot product in a bigger space. (with Part 3 after kernels)

blocks.text: **What it is for:** classification: deciding which of two groups a point belongs to (fraud or genuine, pass or fail, +1 or −1).

**What it does:** many straight lines can separate two groups. SVM picks the one that leaves the **widest gap (margin)** to the nearest points of both groups, like drawing the road between two villages as wide as possible. A wide road means new points are less likely to land on the wrong side (slides p. 6–12).
Three ideas carry the whole chapter

items: **Only the points closest to the road matter.** They are the **support vectors**; every other point could move or vanish without changing the line.
**If the groups overlap a little**, let a few points onto the road but charge a penalty for each: the **soft margin**, with **C** as the price per violation.
**If no straight line works**, lift the data into a space where one does: the **kernel trick**.

lesson.title: Hyperplane, margin and support vectors (p. 6–15)
lesson.lead: Three words you must be able to define and draw.

blocks.text: f(x) = wᵀx + b,   predict sign(f(x))
blocks.caption: w is perpendicular to the line; b shifts it

items: **Hyperplane**: the set wᵀx + b = 0. In 2-D it is a line, w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = 0.
**Margin lines**: wᵀx + b = +1 and wᵀx + b = −1. No training point may sit between them (hard margin).
**Margin width** = distance between the two margin lines = **2/‖w‖**.
**Support vectors**: the training points lying exactly on the margin lines. They alone fix the hyperplane; remove one and the hyperplane moves (p. 13).

blocks.text: distance from point x₀ to the line = |wᵀx₀ + b| / ‖w‖
blocks.caption: so a point with f = ±1 is 1/‖w‖ from the boundary

blocks.text: maximise 2/‖w‖  ⇔  minimise ½‖w‖²

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: Margin **width** is 2/‖w‖. The distance from the boundary to one margin line is 1/‖w‖. If the question just says "margin", write 2/‖w‖ and state that 1/‖w‖ is the half-margin.

blocks.label: Canonical form
blocks.text: Any multiple k·(w, b) gives the same line. SVM fixes the scale by demanding **yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) = 1 exactly on the support vectors**. That is why the exam says "canonical w and b".

lesson.title: Method 1: geometry (the fastest way)
lesson.lead: Use it whenever one support vector per class is given or obvious. Five steps.

items: **Pick the support vectors**: the closest pair of opposite-class points (or the ones the question names). Slide: *Support Vectors* (p. 13).
**Direction**: w points along x⁺ − x⁻, because the boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the pair.
**Scale with p. 16**: *Linear SVM Mathematically* gives w·(x⁺ − x⁻) = 2, so w = 2(x⁺ − x⁻)/‖x⁺ − x⁻‖².
**Bias with p. 21**: b = yᵢ − w·xᵢ for a support vector (use x⁺ with y = +1).
**Check every point** with p. 17: yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1. If one fails, it is also a support vector: use the dual (p. 19–21) or the augmented method (p. 22–32).

blocks.caption: p. 16 and p. 21 of the slides

blocks.text: Two + support vectors and one −
Both + support vectors lie on wᵀx + b = +1, so w ⟂ (x₊₁ − x₊₂). Write w = a·(direction), then solve two equations: f(x₊₁) = 1 and f(x₋) = −1.

blocks.label: Sign check
blocks.text: Always plug a support vector back in. The right line with the wrong sign (w and b both negated) puts every point in the wrong class, and loses the marks for w and b.

lesson.title: Method 2: the dual and Lagrange multipliers (p. 19–21)
lesson.lead: Every constraint gets a multiplier αᵢ ≥ 0. Setting the derivatives to zero gives the two facts the exam uses.

blocks.text: L(w, b, α) = ½‖w‖² − Σ αᵢ [yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) − 1]
∂L/∂w = 0  ⇒  w = Σ αᵢyᵢxᵢ
∂L/∂b = 0  ⇒  Σ αᵢyᵢ = 0

items: **αᵢ > 0 ⇔ support vector.** Points with αᵢ = 0 drop out of w, so moving them (without crossing the margin) changes nothing.
**b from any support vector**: b = yₛ − wᵀxₛ (for a − support vector that is −1 − wᵀxₛ).
**KKT complementary slackness**: αᵢ[yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) − 1] = 0, so either αᵢ = 0 or the point is exactly on the margin.

blocks.text: Recovering α's from a known w (Sourabh P19 type)
Write w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ component by component (two equations in 2-D) and add Σαᵢyᵢ = 0. Three equations, three unknowns. All α's must come out positive.

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: Dropping yᵢ in w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ is the most common mistake. A − support vector contributes **−αᵢxᵢ**.

lesson.lead: Your slides solve for w and b together by adding a 1 to every support vector. Same answer, different book-keeping.

items: Pick the support vectors (p. 22): S1 = (1, 0) negative; S2 = (3, 1), S3 = (3, −1) positive.
Write one equation per support vector, right-hand side = its label: α₁S̃1·S̃i + α₂S̃2·S̃i + α₃S̃3·S̃i = yᵢ.
So w = (1, 0), b = −2: the boundary is **x₁ = 2**, margin 2.

blocks.label: Why α₁ is negative here

lesson.title: Kernels and the kernel trick (p. 48–63)
lesson.lead: If no straight line works, map the data to a space where one does, without ever computing the map.

blocks.text: Map each x to φ(x) in a higher-dimensional space where the classes are linearly separable (p. 52). The dual only ever uses dot products xᵢᵀxⱼ, so replace them with **K(xᵢ, xⱼ) = φ(xᵢ)ᵀφ(xⱼ)**: that is the kernel trick (p. 50, 57–59).

head: Kernel
Formula (p. 60–61)
rows: K(x, z) = (xᵀz + c)ᵖ   (c = 1 on the slides; c = 0 is homogeneous)
K(x, z) = exp(−γ‖x − z‖²)   or   exp(−‖x − z‖²/(2σ²))
K(x, z) = tanh(κxᵀz + θ)  (not always a valid kernel)

blocks.text: 1-D tricks the papers use

items: Labels alternate on a line (+ at odd, − at even): φ(x) = **x mod 2** ⇒ separate with y = 0.5 (2021 Q2, both papers).
+ in the middle, − on both sides: φ(x) = **x²** or **(x − c)²**, then a 1-D threshold in the new space (Sourabh P21, P22).
Find the threshold in the **new** space: midpoint between the largest + value and the smallest − value.

blocks.text: Useful facts

items: Feature-space distance without φ: ‖φ(u) − φ(v)‖² = K(u, u) + K(v, v) − 2K(u, v).
RBF value near 1 ⇒ points similar; near 0 ⇒ far apart.
A valid kernel must give a symmetric, positive semi-definite Gram matrix (Mercer). sin(xᵀz) is **not** valid.
Higher polynomial degree or larger γ ⇒ more flexible boundary ⇒ overfitting risk.

blocks.text: The slides' worked kernel examples (p. 59–61)

items: **2nd-degree map (p. 59):** for K(a, b) = (aᵀb)², φ(x, y) = (x², √2·xy, y²). Check: φ(a)ᵀφ(b) = a₁²b₁² + 2a₁a₂b₁b₂ + a₂²b₂² = (a₁b₁ + a₂b₂)². For the point (2, 3): φ = (4, 6√2, 9).
**Kernel values (p. 61)** for x = (1, 2), y = (2, 3), so xᵀy = 8: linear (q = 1) K = **8**; homogeneous q = 2: K = 8² = **64**; inhomogeneous with c = 1, q = 2: K = (1 + 8)² = **81**.
**Dual with a kernel (p. 63):** maximise Σαᵢ − ½ΣΣαᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼK(xᵢ, xⱼ) subject to αᵢ ≥ 0, Σαᵢyᵢ = 0; predict with f(x) = Σαᵢyᵢ K(xᵢ, x) + b. Only the kernel changes from the linear SVM.

blocks.text: Mercer's condition: which functions are valid kernels? (handout)

K is a valid kernel (it equals φ(x)ᵀφ(z) for some map φ) **if and only if** every Gram matrix it produces is **symmetric** and **positive semi-definite**: for any points x₁ … xₙ, the matrix Gᵢⱼ = K(xᵢ, xⱼ) has all eigenvalues ≥ 0 (equivalently cᵀGc ≥ 0 for every vector c).

items: **Symmetric**: K(x, z) = K(z, x).
**Positive semi-definite**: for two points, K(x, x) ≥ 0, K(z, z) ≥ 0 and K(x, x)K(z, z) − K(x, z)² ≥ 0 (the 2 × 2 determinant).
If any Gram matrix fails, K is **not** a Mercer kernel and the SVM optimisation may have no proper solution.

head: Kernel
Valid (Mercer)?
rows: xᵀz, (xᵀz + c)ᵖ with c ≥ 0, p a positive integer
Sums, positive multiples and products of valid kernels
Only for some κ, θ: not always
**No**: e.g. x = z gives K(x, x) = sin(‖x‖²), which can be negative

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Mercer guarantees the kernel really is a dot product in some feature space, so the SVM problem stays convex with one global optimum. That is the justification for using K without ever computing φ.

blocks.label: Theory point
blocks.text: Kernel SVMs are expensive because they need the n × n kernel (Gram) matrix: time and memory grow with n².

lesson.title: Applications: structured and unstructured data (handout)
lesson.lead: SVM only needs numbers (or a kernel between two items), so it works on tables and, after a suitable representation, on text and images.

head: Structured data
Unstructured data
rows: Rows and columns of numeric or categorical features
Text, images, audio, sequences: no fixed columns
Scale the features (SVM is distance-based), one-hot encode categories, use a linear or RBF kernel
First turn each item into a vector (bag-of-words / TF-IDF, embeddings, image features) or use a kernel that compares items directly (string kernels)
Linear for many features; RBF for curved boundaries
Linear for text (very high-dimensional, usually separable); RBF / polynomial for images
Loan default and credit risk, fraud detection, churn, medical diagnosis from test values
Spam and text categorisation (Joachims, slides p. 67), sentiment, handwritten digits, face detection, protein classification

items: **Text** is the classic SVM success: thousands of word features, few examples, and the classes are usually linearly separable in that space.
**Mixed data** (e.g. transaction amounts plus remarks text, as in Mar 2026 makeup Q7): combine numeric features with text embeddings and use a kernel SVM; the cost is the n × n kernel matrix.
Always **scale** numeric features: a feature with a large range otherwise dominates wᵀx and the distances inside RBF.

head: Question says…
Write this
rows: Closest opposite pair → w ∥ x₊ − x₋ → w·(x⁺ − x⁻) = 2 (p. 16) → b = y − w·x (p. 21) → check all yᵢf ≥ 1 (p. 17) → margin 2/‖w‖ (p. 16)
Check Σαᵢyᵢ = 0 → w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ → b = yₛ − wᵀxₛ (agree for every SV) → margin
Verify yₛf(xₛ) = 1 → components of w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ plus Σαᵢyᵢ = 0 → solve
Support vector? / y·f ≥ 1? → say unchanged or changed, with the reason
min ½‖w‖² + one constraint per point, with numbers (+ ξᵢ and C for soft margin)
"Not linearly separable, use the kernel trick"
Name φ, tabulate φ(x), find the threshold in the new space, map back
"Which model overfits / what does C do"
Large train–test gap ⇒ overfit; large C or high degree ⇒ complex boundary

items: Show f(x) for every point when you check: it earns method marks.

worked.title: Geometry · MFML Feb 2026 Q5: two separating lines (8 marks)

problem.text: +1: X1 (2, 2), X2 (4, 4). −1: X3 (2, 0), X4 (4, 0). (a) Write the hard-margin primal. (b) Show x₂ = 1 separates the data. (c) Show x₂ − x₁ = −1 separates the data. (d) Find the margin of each and say which is better.

steps.label: Slide formulas
steps.text: Use: *Solving the Optimization Problem* (p. 17–18); *Linear SVM Mathematically* (p. 16); *Line with 2 features: R2* (p. 14).

steps.label: (a) Primal
steps.text: min ½(w₁² + w₂²) subject to 2w₁ + 2w₂ + b ≥ 1, 4w₁ + 4w₂ + b ≥ 1, −(2w₁ + b) ≥ 1, −(4w₁ + b) ≥ 1.

steps.label: (c) x₂ − x₁ = −1
steps.text: w = (−1, 1), b = 1, f = x₂ − x₁ + 1: X1 1, X2 1; X3 −1, X4 −3. It separates.

steps.label: (d) Margins
steps.text: Both are already canonical (closest points give f = ±1). x₂ = 1: ‖w‖ = 1 ⇒ margin **2**. x₂ − x₁ = −1: ‖w‖ = √2 ⇒ margin 2/√2 ≈ **1.414**.

steps.label: (d) Better
steps.text: **x₂ = 1** has the wider margin, so SVM prefers it. (It is the true maximum: the gap between (2, 2) and (2, 0) is exactly 2.)

worked.title: Geometry · Mar 2026 makeup Q7: two support vectors (8 marks)

problem.text: P1 (1, 4) +1, P2 (2, 3) +1, P3 (4, 1) −1, P4 (5, 2) −1. Only P2 and P3 are support vectors. (a) Hyperplane by geometry. (b) Canonical w, b and f(x). (c) Which αᵢ mark a support vector? (d) ‖w‖ and margin. (e) Why can kernel SVMs be expensive?

steps.label: Slide formulas
steps.text: Use: *Linear SVM Mathematically* (p. 16); *Solving the Optimization Problem* (p. 21); *Solving the Optimization Problem* (p. 19); *Examples of Kernel Functions* (p. 60).

steps.label: (a)
steps.text: Perpendicular bisector of P2–P3: midpoint (3, 2); P2 − P3 = (−2, 2) ⇒ w ∥ (−1, 1). Boundary −x₁ + x₂ + 1 = 0, i.e. **x₂ = x₁ − 1**.

steps.label: (b) Check
steps.text: f(x) = −0.5x₁ + 0.5x₂ + 0.5: P2 +1, P3 −1, P1 +2, P4 −1. All yᵢf ≥ 1 ✓ (P4 sits exactly on the margin too).

steps.label: (c)
steps.text: Support vector ⇔ **αᵢ > 0**. w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ, so points with αᵢ = 0 contribute nothing: only P2 and P3 shape the classifier.

steps.label: (d)
steps.text: ‖w‖ = √0.5 = **0.707**; margin = 2/‖w‖ = **2.83** (= distance P2–P3). Wider margin ⇒ more robust to noise.

steps.label: (e)
steps.text: The n × n kernel matrix: time and memory grow with n². (sin(xᵀz) is not a valid kernel.)

formulas.name: Line ↔ hyperplane
formulas.formula: ax + cy + b = 0 ⇔ w·x + b = 0, w = [a, c]

formulas.name: Constraints and primal
formulas.formula: positive: w·xᵢ + b ≥ 1; negative: w·xᵢ + b ≤ −1; min ½wᵀw s.t. yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1

formulas.name: Lagrangian and its derivatives
formulas.formula: L = ½‖w‖² − Σαᵢ[yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) − 1]; ∂L/∂w = 0 ⇒ w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ; ∂L/∂b = 0 ⇒ Σαᵢyᵢ = 0

formulas.name: Bias and classification
formulas.formula: b = yᵢ − w·xᵢ (any support vector); f(x) = sign(w·x + b) = sign(Σαᵢyᵢ xᵢ·x + b)

formulas.name: Support vectors
formulas.formula: non-zero αᵢ ⇒ support vector; f(x) = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢᵀx + b

formulas.name: Augmented method
formulas.formula: add 1 as bias input; α₁S̃1·S̃i + α₂S̃2·S̃i + α₃S̃3·S̃i = label; last entry of w̃ is b
formulas.note: Slide: Numerical Example, Steps 1–8 (p. 22–32); Solving for α (p. 34–35)

formulas.name: Soft-margin primal
formulas.formula: min ½‖w‖² + CΣξᵢ s.t. yᵢwᵀxᵢ ≥ 1 − ξᵢ, ξᵢ ≥ 0
formulas.note: Slide: Soft Margin (p. 41) and Hard Margin vs Soft Margin (p. 42)

formulas.name: Role of C
formulas.formula: large C: slacks cost more, misclassification not OK (narrow margin); low C: misclassification OK, large margin; C controls overfitting
formulas.note: Slide: Slack Variable (p. 40) and Effect of Margin size v/s misclassification cost (p. 43–46)

formulas.name: Feature map
formulas.formula: map x to a higher dimension (e.g. x → (x, x²)) where the data is separable

formulas.name: Kernel
formulas.formula: K(xᵢ, xⱼ) = φ(xᵢ)ᵀφ(xⱼ)

formulas.name: 2nd-degree map
formulas.formula: φ(x, y) = (x², √2xy, y²) for K = (aᵀb)²

formulas.name: Kernel functions
formulas.formula: linear xᵢᵀxⱼ; polynomial (1 + xᵢᵀxⱼ)ᵖ; Gaussian exp(−‖xᵢ − xⱼ‖²/(2σ²)); sigmoid tanh(β₀xᵢᵀxⱼ + β₁)

formulas.name: Polynomial kernel forms
formulas.formula: homogeneous (xᵀy)^q; inhomogeneous (c + xᵀy)^q

formulas.name: Dual with a kernel
formulas.formula: L(α) = Σαᵢ − ½ΣΣαᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼK(xᵢ, xⱼ); f(x) = Σαᵢyᵢ K(xᵢ, x) + b
